name: active-record
intent: Make a domain object the record for one database row: keep the row's state, row-local behavior, and the methods that find and persist it together, so a small domain does not pay for a separate mapping layer.
problem: A simple relational domain still needs a choice about where persistence lives. A Data Mapper or gateway separates table I/O from the object but adds mapping code and a second place to navigate, while direct SQL leaks schema knowledge into callers; the recurring question is whether one row object can own its data and CRUD without hiding transaction boundaries or pretending to model cross-row rules.
context: A relational store is the single system of record, the domain is small and its rules are mostly local to one row (validation, derivations, simple state transitions), and the team prefers a convention-driven persistence layer over a designed one. Typical homes are framework ecosystems where the ORM is the house style (Rails, Laravel Eloquent, Django, GORM, Vapor Fluent, TypeORM), CRUD-heavy applications, and thin layers over an already well-shaped legacy schema. Entity Framework Core can host behavior on entity classes, but its DbContext and mapping conventions are a Data Mapper-shaped boundary rather than pure Active Record. It stops applying as soon as invariants span several objects, several representations of one table are needed, or the store must be swappable.
benefits: A domain object is one artefact: row data, the logic on that data and the methods that persist it can be read, changed and reviewed together, with no mapper to keep in sync.
Dramatically less code and ceremony for simple domains - no mapping classes, no repository, no unit of work; the schema's shape is directly readable in the class.
Conventions (class -> table, attribute -> column, primary key and timestamp columns) remove most configuration, so a new table becomes a new class plus a migration.
Abstraction in the direction the application actually uses it: callers ask an object for its own data instead of assembling queries, which keeps single-row operations short and legible.

Frameworks that ship it (Rails, Django, GORM, Fluent) add migrations, validations, callbacks and associations for free, giving a small team production-grade persistence without a persistence architecture.

Natural first refactoring step: a row can start as an Active Record and later be extracted into a Data Mapper or Repository once the domain earns it, because the tabular structure is already explicit.
tradeoffs: Business logic cannot be exercised without a database (or a mocked persistence layer), so domain rules end up tested through the persistence stack and test suites get slow and brittle.
Class, table and columns become one coupled artefact: renaming a column, changing a type or splitting a table ripples into the code that holds the rules, not just into a mapper.

The class carries two responsibilities - domain behaviour and persistence - and bloats as the domain grows; the pattern is explicitly less suitable for complex domain logic, and the escape hatch is usually inheritance the framework provides, which is harder to compose than delegation.
Persistence is decided per object: each save is its own transaction unless the caller wraps one, so multi-row invariants can be violated by two successful saves and no layer enforces atomicity.

Unloaded or partially loaded objects are dangerous: saving an instance that was never read writes stale or default values over columns it does not know about, and concurrent edits silently overwrite each other unless a version column is added.
Hidden query cost: association access, lazy relations and finder calls in loops emit queries (N+1) that are invisible in the domain code and show up only under load.
Validation and mapping rules tend to be duplicated between the object, the database constraints and any reporting consumer of the same tables.

participants.responsibility: The domain object itself: its class maps to one table, each instance maps to one row, and it carries the row's data, the domain logic on that data and the CRUD methods that persist itself (save/update/delete).
Class-level or manager-level lookup (find, byId, objects.filter, Model.query) that reconstitutes record objects from rows; deliberately row-shaped instead of a composable query object.
The relational structure the class mirrors; table name, primary key and column names are tied to the object by convention or by mapping attributes, replacing an explicit mapper.
Primary key (and optional lock-version/timestamp columns) that let an instance know whether it is new or persisted, and let conflicting writes be detected instead of blindly overwriting.
The handle through which the object reads and writes itself (connection, session, EntityManager, DataSource); its scope also decides whether several saves form one transaction.

use_cases: CRUD-heavy applications where most screens and endpoints map onto a single table: forms, admin back offices, catalogs, content management.
Small-to-medium domains whose rules are mostly per-row - field validation, derived values, one-row state transitions - so a mapper layer would move data around without adding a model.
Prototypes and thin service layers over an existing, already normalised legacy schema where the table shape is stable and the domain is the schema.
Framework-default persistence: a Rails, Django, GORM, Vapor Fluent or TypeORM codebase where fighting the ORM for purity costs more than it returns.
Simple record-shaped bounded contexts inside a larger system - settings, audit entries, lookup tables - where a full domain model would be overhead.
JSON:API or REST backends for SPAs and mobile apps where the data model maps directly to a relational schema with minimal transformation.
Microservices with a single-responsibility data store: a service whose entire bounded context is one aggregate root table or a handful of tightly coupled tables.
Batch import pipelines where records are validated once and bulk-inserted (insert_all/upsert_all), and the domain logic has already been applied before the bulk operation.
Multi-tenant SaaS backends where row-level isolation is enforced at the database and the ORM connection handles tenant scoping automatically.

Real Rails systems such as GitLab and Discourse are good fits for row-shaped users, posts, permissions and settings backed by PostgreSQL; keep their reporting and cross-record workflows in query or service boundaries.

A Django or Laravel CRUD surface such as an admin or back-office module fits when each request mostly validates, loads, changes and saves one model; switch to a mapper or repository when the same data feeds materially different contracts.
avoid_when: Invariants span several records or aggregates: use a Data Mapper plus Unit of Work so one domain model can enforce consistency and one commit can coordinate all writes; add a Repository when callers need a persistence boundary.
One table feeds materially different views (web form, report, message): use a Data Mapper or row/table gateway per representation instead of making one Active Record class carry every projection.

The store is non-relational, polyglot or deliberately swappable (document store, event log, multiple databases): use a Data Mapper or Repository, or an explicit gateway, so domain objects do not decide storage shape.
Every read/write must pass central tenancy, authorization, caching or sharding policy: use a Repository or gateway as the enforceable choke point rather than duplicating policy across record classes.

Aggregations, window functions, CTEs and reporting dominate: use first-class query objects or a Transaction Script with SQL, keeping Active Record for row updates, instead of forcing set-shaped work through object loops.
Several applications own one schema: use migration ownership plus a gateway or Data Mapper boundary; independent Active Record conventions and migrations will compete for the same tables.

Pure unit testing of rich domain rules is a hard requirement: use a Data Mapper/domain model or extract rules into plain objects, because Active Record couples those rules to a database/session or test double.
anti_patterns: Using record objects as the whole domain model: single-table CRUD classes slowly acquire cross-object workflow until the application logic lives in persistence objects no one can test.
Load-one-column, save-the-whole-object: reading a row to change one field and writing the instance back, silently overwriting concurrent changes (no version column, no partial update).
Looping over associations to build an object graph - the N+1 pattern - and calling it the ORM's cost instead of a design choice.
Finder methods that concatenate user input into SQL strings, turning the pattern's convenience into an injection surface.
Assuming save() is atomic with respect to other saves: several record writes that must succeed or fail together are executed without an explicit transaction.
Bypassing the object for 'performance' and issuing ad-hoc SQL from callers, so the schema knowledge the class was supposed to own now lives everywhere.

Ghost objects from lazy-loaded proxies: accessing an unloaded belongs_to association before assigning it produces a nil-like proxy that silently passes nil checks but raises on access, hiding bugs in conditional logic.
Fighting the ORM's lazy-loading defaults by scattering includes/preload/eager_load calls across every controller, rather than centralising data-access design in query objects.
Using find_each/find_in_batches for iteration and assuming the ordering is preserved when it is silently replaced by primary-key iteration.
design_principles: Single responsibility at row granularity: a record owns its data, the behaviour over that data, and its own persistence - and nothing that reaches across rows.
Convention over configuration: derive the mapping (table name, primary key, timestamps, column names) mechanically so there is no mapping code to maintain.
Explicit atomicity: because persistence is decided per object, the transaction boundary belongs to the caller and must be stated wherever invariants cross objects.
Keep the mapping declarative and inspectable: what the class means in the database should be readable from the class, not reconstructed from query strings.
Choose the pattern for the scale of the domain: Active Record is the small-domain default, and the principled exit is Data Mapper/Repository, not a growing record class.
best_practices: Keep record classes thin - validation, derivations and small state transitions - and move workflow that spans records into service objects.
Know the persistence state of every instance (new, loaded, stub) and save only the columns you actually changed where the library allows it (update_fields, AsChangeset, save_changes, dirty tracking).
Add a version column (lock_version, @Version, rowversion) and treat the conflict it surfaces as a domain case rather than letting the last writer win.
Wrap logically coupled saves in one explicit transaction; if that happens often, the design wants a Unit of Work.
Never build SQL from string interpolation - use bound parameters, and keep raw SQL confined to the finder methods of the record class.
Load associations deliberately (eager loading / includes / preload / eager_load) instead of navigating relations inside loops to prevent N+1 queries.
Keep domain rules testable without a database by extracting the rule into a plain object or by running against a temporary in-memory instance of the real engine.

Use after_commit or after_rollback callbacks for side effects that must survive the commit (e.g., enqueuing a background job, publishing an event) rather than after_save or after_update which fire inside the transaction.
Prefer scopes and class methods for building query fragments rather than scattering where() calls through controllers or service objects.
Isolate tests with DatabaseCleaner or transactional rollback so each test runs against a clean, independent dataset without shared state.
Reserve callbacks for framework lifecycle events (timestamps, slug generation); move business rule triggers into explicit service calls or domain events to keep behaviour visible and testable.
In DDD-oriented codebases, treat the record as a persistence mechanism for an aggregate root and keep all domain logic in the aggregate itself, using the record only for loading and saving.
For bulk writes (imports, seeds) prefer the ORM's bulk insert method (insert_all, upsert_all, createMany) over a save loop, but verify that no load-bearing callbacks are being skipped.
Use pluck/pluck_hash over map(&:attribute) to avoid instantiating full model objects when only column values are needed.
Monitor query volume per request (Bullet, Scout, Prosopite, or database query logs) to catch N+1 patterns before they reach production.
For large dataset iteration use find_each/find_in_batches but be aware it silently re-orders by primary key; use cursor-based pagination when order matters.

Drop to raw SQL (or the framework's native SQL escape hatch) for genuinely SQL-shaped problems: aggregations, window functions, CTEs, complex reporting - the ORM query builder is not the right tool for every query.

Use explicit connection pool sizing and set isolation levels per transaction rather than relying on framework defaults, which differ across databases (READ COMMITTED in PostgreSQL vs REPEATABLE READ in MySQL InnoDB).

related_patterns_notes.data-mapper: Keeps persistence in a separate mapper, leaving domain objects independent of table I/O; Active Record deliberately combines the two.
related_patterns_notes.row-data-gateway: Puts CRUD for one row in a gateway object rather than on the row itself; Active Record puts those operations on the record.
related_patterns_notes.table-data-gateway: Exposes table-level operations through one gateway, not per-row objects; Active Record returns row objects with their own persistence.
related_patterns_notes.repository: Presents collection or aggregate persistence behind a boundary; unlike Active Record, the model need not save itself.
related_patterns_notes.unit-of-work: Collects multiple changes and commits them together; Active Record alone has no cross-object coordination.
related_patterns_notes.transaction-script: Keeps each use-case workflow in a procedure; Active Record keeps row-local behavior on the record.
related_patterns_notes.domain-model: Models rich business rules independently of persistence; Active Record couples row data and CRUD to the table.
related_patterns_notes.lazy-load: Defers related data until access; it can be used with Active Record but is not the persistence pattern itself.
